title: Chemistry 11 — Chapter 11: The Sealed Container
description: A sealed gas canister is overdue for inspection, and the reading doesn't match the manifest. Work through kinetic theory, pressure units, and the single-variable gas laws before signing off.

mika.name: Ms. Mika Tan
mika.description: Won't sign off on anything until the numbers actually check out.

dev.name: Dev
dev.description: Assumes gas behavior is basically unpredictable.

kmt_notes.name: Kinetic Theory Notes
kmt_notes.description: The core assumptions behind ideal gas behavior.

gas_laws_sheet.name: Gas Laws Reference Sheet
gas_laws_sheet.description: Boyle's, Charles's, Gay-Lussac's, and the combined gas law, all in one place.

elements.text: This canister was sealed at room temperature, but it's been sitting near the radiator all week. The manifest pressure doesn't match today's reading.
Gases are just unpredictable, right? Maybe it's fine.

elements.prompt: Mika hands you the kinetic theory notes.

options.text: "Not unpredictable at all — gas behavior follows kinetic theory exactly. Let's work through it."

elements.text: Kinetic molecular theory treats gas particles as constantly moving, colliding elastically, with negligible volume and no attraction between them. Temperature is directly tied to their average kinetic energy — heat a gas up, and its particles move faster and hit the container walls harder and more often.

config.question: According to kinetic molecular theory, what happens to the average kinetic energy of gas particles as temperature increases?
config.explanation: Temperature is a direct measure of average kinetic energy in kinetic molecular theory — higher temperature means faster-moving particles.

config.prompt: Sort each statement by whether it matches the assumptions of kinetic molecular theory.

items.text: Gas particles are in constant, random motion
Gas particles take up significant volume relative to the container
Gas particles strongly attract one another

elements.text: Pressure shows up in a few different units here — kPa, atm, and mmHg all measure the same thing. Standard atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa, which equals exactly 1 atm, which equals 760 mmHg.

config.prompt: Standard atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa. Rounded to the nearest whole number, how many mmHg is that?

config.question: Which of these is NOT equal to standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm)?
config.explanation: 1 atm is exactly 101.3 kPa, not 100.0 kPa — a close but incorrect rounding.

elements.text: Charles's Law relates volume and temperature at constant pressure: V1/T1 = V2/T2. It only works with absolute temperature — Kelvin, never Celsius.

config.question: Charles's Law calculations require temperature to be expressed in:
config.explanation: Gas law ratios only work correctly with an absolute temperature scale, since Celsius and Fahrenheit have arbitrary (non-zero) starting points.

config.prompt: A gas occupies 2.00 L at 300 K. At constant pressure, using V1/T1 = V2/T2, what volume (in L) will it occupy at 450 K?

block4_boyle_combined.title: Boyle's, Gay-Lussac's, and the Combined Law

elements.text: Boyle's Law relates pressure and volume at constant temperature: P1V1 = P2V2. Gay-Lussac's relates pressure and temperature at constant volume: P1/T1 = P2/T2. When all three — pressure, volume, and temperature — can change at once, use the combined gas law: P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2.

config.question: Which gas law applies to a problem involving pressure and volume changing at constant temperature?
config.explanation: Boyle's Law is specifically pressure-volume at constant temperature — P1V1 = P2V2.

config.prompt: A gas at 100 kPa occupies 4.00 L. At constant temperature, using Boyle's Law P1V1 = P2V2, what pressure (in kPa) is needed to compress it to 2.00 L?

elements.text: Kinetic theory, pressure units, and every gas law check out. Safe to sign off — the canister is behaving exactly as predicted.
We got there, but a step or two needs review. Let's revisit which law applies when before the next inspection.

elements.prompt: The inspection form is ready. What now?

options.text: Walk Dev through why gas behavior is completely predictable once you know which law fits which situation.
Sign off and move on. Good enough for today.

elements.text: So it's not random at all — kinetic theory explains why it happens, and the right gas law nails down exactly how much. I was overcomplicating it.

ending.title: Gas Law Inspector
ending.description: Explained the canister's behavior from kinetic theory and correctly applied every single-variable gas law, teaching Dev to pick the right one.

ending.title: Inspection Signed
ending.description: The canister passed inspection. The deeper gas-law reasoning can wait.
